title: Lending pool burst arbiter PRD - wip
body:
Quick summary:

This doc sketches a lightweight 'lending pool' that lets underutilized dedicated tenants lend ephemeral burst capacity to other tenants via a Burst Arbiter. Goal is to reduce wasted headroom and give predictable, controllable bursts without hard preemption or aggressive evictions. Document captures behavioral contracts, API primitives, bookkeeping (credit escrow), safety leash, telemetry, and rollout plan.

Context / why this exists:
- Many Dedicated pools run with deliberately conservative headroom; during diurnal troughs there's spare capacity.
- Customers want burstability for unpredictable events (campaign spikes, demo days) without buying a permanent larger reservation.
- Current burst options (soft-burst + preemption) are too binary: either no burst or full eviction on conflict. We need a more economically fair, operationally safe fabric.

High-level idea:
- Each Dedicated pool exposes a local lending pool (LP) ledger. Tenants can opt-in to lend a small fraction of reserved capacity in exchange for credits. Borrowers draw from an arbiter that aggregates LPs and enforces per-tenant SLO fingers.
- Lending is time-boxed and revocable with a safety leash: lenders can opt to recall capacity with N-minute notice; arbiter respects higher-priority flows and auto-reconciles debts.

Goals:
- Increase effective utilization of Dedicated clusters by ~10–20% during typical weekday troughs without impacting SLAs for lenders.
- Provide a predictable, auditable credit accounting model (borrow -> repay or pay penalty).
- Keep evictions graceful and explainable to customers; avoid silent QoS loss.

Non-goals:
- This is not a replacement for Reserved Capacity purchases.
- Not intended for untrusted multi-tenant oversubscription where cross-tenant data locality or HW affinity is strict; targeted to pools with compatible model families and latency headroom.

Key primitives and terms (rough):
- Lender token: tenant opt-in config; percent of reserved CPUs/GPUs offered to pool and maximum concurrent lendable fraction.
- Borrow credit: atomic unit consumed when borrower uses borrowed capacity (measured in GPU-seconds or token-credits).
- Arbiter: control plane service that authorizes borrow requests, enforces per-tenant quotas and priority policies, and writes to the escrow ledger.
- Debt window: period (e.g., 24h) in which borrowers must repay via usage credits or billed overage.
- Safety leash: preemption notice period (configurable 1–15m) during which borrower must drain or fallback to a lower-fidelity model.

Behavioral contracts:
- Borrower requests X units for T seconds. Arbiter evaluates against: pool available lendable units, borrower priority tier, outstanding debt, and predicted lender recall probability. If allowed, arbiter returns a short-lived grant token with an expiration and recall window.
- Lenders retain right to recall up to Y% of lent capacity. Recall triggers a grace timer (safety leash).
- If borrower cannot release capacity within leash, arbiter will initiate controlled downgrade: shift models to quantized variants, reduce concurrency, then escalate to preemption.

Credit accounting model (sketch):
- Borrow credit accrues at time-of-use. Borrowers earn temporary 'burst-credit balance' and must reconcile before debt window closes.
- Lenders receive credits into their account proportional to contributed capacity * time. Credits can be redeemed for discounts on future bills or used to buy mitigation (e.g., faster recall notice).
- Option for cash settlement: if borrower fails to repay within window, charge overage at elevated rate.

Policy knobs for productization:
- Max lend fraction per tenant (configurable per contract).
- Pool-level concurrency cap for borrowed workloads to avoid latency storms.
- Priority weighting: customer tier mapping -> borrow preemption priority.
- Auto-recall aggressiveness metric derived from telemetry (ramp up when lender's trailing P99 > threshold).

APIs / UX (quick notes):
- GET /v1/dedicated/pools/{pool_id}/lending-status -> returns available capacity, active grants, latency health signals.
- POST /v1/dedicated/borrow -> {pool_id, tenant_id, requested_units, duration_hint, fallback_policy} -> returns grant token OR reason code.
- POST /v1/dedicated/return -> {grant_token, actual_usage_seconds} -> reconciles ledger.
- Webhook: POST to tenant endpoint when recall is initiated {grant_token, recall_eta_seconds, suggested-fallback}.
- Console: lending dashboard for tenants with earned credits, active loans, and recall history.

Operational considerations / telemetry:
- Track per-grant: submit_ts, granted_units, recall_events, reclaim_latency, final_outcome (released|downgraded|preempted).
- Pool-level metrics: lendable_utilization, borrowed_utilization, recall_rate, failed_release_rate, average grace drain time.
- Billing metrics: credits_issued, credits_redeemed, overage_charges.
- Alerts: recall_rate spike on a pool, failed_release_rate > 5% for >15m, borrowed_utilization > safety_ratio.

Fall back strategies for borrowers on recall:
- Graceful reduce concurrency -> fallback to queued requests -> drop to quantized model variant -> (last resort) preempt. Document per-model downgrade recipes in Optimize.

Security and isolation notes:
- Borrowed capacity must never allow cross-tenant data leakage; enforce standard tenant network and workload sandboxing. Borrowed tasks must remain in the borrower's execution namespace.
- Borrow grants are control-plane only; scheduling still uses existing node-level affinity and sandboxing.

SLO impact analysis (expected):
- Lender: no change to median latency; risk limited to P95/P99 tail if recall thresholds mis-configured. Mitigation: conservative default max-lend 10% and aggressive telemetry.
- Borrower: best-effort burst SLO with explicit fallbacks; must design clients to accept downgrade.

Cost / economics thought experiment:
- Example: 10 lenders each lending 5% of pool = effective 50% extra transient headroom; if usage shifts to borrowers rather than idle, platform utilization improves and lenders get discounts equal to credits earned.
- Need simulation to convert GPU-seconds to monetary credits and test fairness across tenant sizes.

Rollout plan (phased):
1) Lab prototype: single pool, internal tenants only. Manual arbiter, disabled auto-recall.
2) Pilot: opt-in with 3 customers, full arbiter, telemetry + billing path enabled but auto-recall conservative. 6–8 week pilot.
3) Scale: expand to pools with compatible model families; expose tenant console and API.

Open questions / riskiest assumptions:
- How to price credits so lenders feel compensated but borrowers aren't discouraged? (pricing elasticity unknown).
- Can we safely predict recall risk well enough to avoid P99 regressions for lenders? Need ML-based lender health prediction or very conservative defaults.
- Legal/billing: are credits considered discounts or separate invoice line? How to show to enterprise finance?

Next steps / TODOs:
- Simulation task: convert 30 days of pool telemetry into simulated lending scenarios (owner: Marcus). Jira: DCP-789.
- Design: finalize recall/handshake API and webhook payload (owner: Asha).
- UX: draft console mockups for lending dashboard (owner: Claire).
- Legal: surface billing representation options for credits (owner: Priya).

Notes to self / loose thoughts:
- Consider a 'greenband' where lenders get higher compensation if they mark capacity as non-recallable during business hours (longer commitment windows).
- Think about inter-pool lending across AZs with synchronous cross-pool arbitration — high complexity, defer.
- Could integrate with Optimize to recommend which tenants should lend based on historical idle profiles.

If this idea looks promising, next doc: formal PRD with precise policy math, API contract, simulation results, and patch-level rollout playbook.

-- Diego
